title: Getting ready
hookLine: Friday is for cooking, cleaning and washing, as if a guest were coming
last: HOLY TIME — A PALACE IN TIME.

cards: One hour before guests arrive, the vacuum comes out. Someone shoves mail into a drawer. The good towels go in the bathroom.

Somebody's in the shower, somebody's stirring a pot, and the house smells like onions and soap. It's chaos, and it's also a kind of love. In homes that keep Shabbat, that's Friday afternoon, week after week.
Someone important is coming at sundown, and the someone is a day.

teach.b: Erev means evening, or eve. Erev Shabbat is Friday, especially Friday afternoon. The roots go back to the manna.

teach.h: TWICE AS MUCH ON THE SIXTH DAY.
teach.b: On the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much and prepared what they brought in, so there'd be food on the seventh. Getting ready is built into the very first Shabbat.

teach.h: THE RABBIS DID THEIR OWN CHORES.
teach.b: The Talmud tells how the great rabbis spent Friday, and they weren't too important for chores. One singed the head of an animal for cooking. Another salted a fish.
Another cut beets; another carried loads in and out of the house. They did it themselves, on purpose, because honoring Shabbat with your own hands was part of it.

teach.h: GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.
teach.b: And as the sun went down, one sage would wrap himself in his cloak, stand, and say: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the queen. Another would say: come in, O bride.
Centuries later, a Friday night song welcoming the Sabbath bride grew from those words.

So in many homes, Friday's list goes something like this: cook the meals, because Shabbat has no cooking; clean; set the table with a white cloth; bathe; put on something nice; turn off whatever needs turning off.
Some people get ready for hours. Some just do one thing. Either way, it's the idea behind any dinner party.
When a guest you love is coming, you don't wait until they're at the door to get ready.

how: In many Jewish homes, Friday is spent cooking the Shabbat meals in advance, cleaning, setting a festive table, bathing and dressing up before candle lighting at sundown.

games.q: you're a well-known rabbi in Babylonia. it's Friday afternoon, and you have students who could do the chores for you. what do you do?
o: prepare something with your own hands.
games.why: the Talmud tells of great sages salting fish and singeing meat themselves: honoring Shabbat with your own hands was the point.

practice: Picture the room you'll be in on Friday evening, and find one surface in it: a table, a counter, a nightstand, even the home screen of your phone.
Picture it clear, with something small and good placed on it: a cloth, a candle, a plate, a flower. That surface is where the guest arrives.

wordCard.voice: Erev Shabbat. The eve of the Sabbath: Friday, when homes cook, clean and wash to greet the day like an honored guest.

orig.note: Hebrew: the eve of Shabbat. erev is the same word as evening in Genesis 1.

carryVoice: Your line: get ready for a guest. The chores are part of the welcome. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119a (the sages prepare; greeting the Sabbath queen and bride)
